_meta.provenance: Sampled from the LIVE site https://frontaliereticino.ch. 900 pages fetched with curl (all HTTP 200); node was used only to parse locally-saved HTML.
_meta.population: The 25 sitemap-jobs-<canton>.xml files listed in /sitemap.xml enumerate 29,835 job-detail URLs = 7,457 jobs x 4 locale slots (it/en/de/fr).
_meta.sampling: 300 IT job pages drawn by seeded shuffle over all 7,457 jobs; for the first 150 jobs the en/de/fr alternates were also fetched, giving 150 complete quadruples (600 slots). Corpus de-duplicated to one entry per (normalised title + targetLocale) so no employer template dominates. Selection is trap-weighted, so class balance here does NOT reflect the site-wide defect rate (measured separately: ~25% of IT slots, ~13% of EN, ~11% of FR, 0% of DE).
_meta.titleField: JSON-LD JobPosting.title. On this site that field already equals <h1 class=hero-title> MINUS the " — Company" suffix, so no stripping was needed and none was applied — titles are verbatim. company/location are emitted separately so an implementer can reconstruct the h1 and check that their rule ignores the employer name.
_meta.htmlGotcha: In the served HTML, attributes are UNQUOTED: <h1 class=hero-title>, <link rel=alternate hreflang=de href="...">. A regex expecting hreflang="de" silently matches nothing.

labellingRule.method: Language-independent. Both the German and the French marker sets are run against EVERY title regardless of which language the posting was thought to originate in. sourceLang is a reported attribute, never an input to the label — an earlier draft inferred it from the canton language zone and consequently mislabelled a German title on a Ticino page as clean.
labellingRule.broken_true: After (a) removing gender codes in parentheses, bare integers and percentages, and (b) removing an allowlist of Swiss toponyms, employer names and brands, the title still contains one of: a German word from a curated UNAMBIGUOUS list, a token carrying ä/ö/ü/ß, a German inclusive-gender artefact (":in", "*in", "_in", ":r", ":innen"), or a French common word — and targetLocale is not that language.
labellingRule.german_wordlist_note: The German word list deliberately EXCLUDES English/French homographs (still, organisation, administration, disposition, restauration, region, monteur, koch, interesse). Including them raised the false-positive rate on correct English and Italian titles. This trades recall for precision on purpose.
deliberate_clean_calls: Gender CODES left in the wrong locale (m/w/d, w/m/d in a non-German title; h/f, f/h in a non-French one) are recorded in notes[] but labelled broken:false. They are a locale inconsistency, not a wrong-language title, and flagging them would raise the false-positive rate against otherwise-correct titles. Opt in via notes[] if you want to treat them as defects.
English borrowings that are normal in Italian job ads (manager, marketing, IT, store, retail, shift, data center, business, compliance, officer, project manager) are labelled broken:false.

Titles carrying German PROPER NOUNS (Zürich Nord, Grüze Park Winterthur, Stazione di Ricerca Früebüel) are labelled broken:false — they are the deliberate traps for a naive "non-ASCII => German" rule.
isSourceSlot:true entries are the posting in its own source language, correct by construction, included as guaranteed negatives.
labellingRule.excluded: English CALQUES such as "Software Ingegnere", "Senior Electronics Ingegnere", "Database Infrastructure Specialista" were removed from the corpus entirely. They are a real defect but a DIFFERENT one (word-level substitution producing ungrammatical Italian), and labelling them either way would corrupt a wrong-language benchmark.

fields.title: verbatim JobPosting.title of THIS slot
fields.sourceTitle: same field on the source-locale slot; null when that slot was not fetched (jobs 150-299 of the sample)
fields.sourceLang: de|fr|it, reported not asserted; see labellingRule.method
fields.targetLocale: it|en|de|fr, the locale of the page this title was served on
fields.notes: weak signals deliberately NOT part of the label
fields.isSourceSlot: true when this slot is the posting in its own language

knownWeaknesses: The French marker list is much smaller than the German one, so recall on French residue is lower than on German residue; FR-source breakage is under-represented.
The toponym/employer allowlist was built from the observed sample and is not exhaustive; an unseen Swiss place name carrying an umlaut would produce a false broken:true.
sourceLang for entries where no marker fired still derives from the canton language zone (Grigioni and Vallese forced to "de"), so it can be wrong on clean entries. Do not train on sourceLang.
Near-duplicate employer templates were collapsed, so per-employer frequency in this file is not the site-wide frequency.
_meta.caveat: These labels are lexical/heuristic ground truth produced by automated sampling of the live site, not human-verified translation judgements. Every label was assigned by regex-based marker rules over a proper-noun allowlist, then spot-checked by eye on the top offenders and on each trap category — the corpus as a whole was NOT read and adjudicated entry by entry by a fluent speaker of all four languages. Expect a residue of misclassification in both directions, particularly on very short titles, on mixed-language titles where the correct rendering is genuinely debatable (English job-title borrowings above all), and on entries whose true source language differs from the canton language zone. Treat this as a calibration corpus for tuning and regression-testing a detector, not as an authoritative gold set: if a new rule disagrees with a label here, open the URL and read the page before assuming the rule is wrong.

revisions.why: A sweep of ALL 79,754 non-source title slots in data/jobs/by-crawler found three false-positive families in the detector lexicon that 179 entries cannot expose, and the labelling rule in _meta.labellingRule shared two of them: it, too, counted the German article "des" and the German quantifier "alle" as German evidence. Eight entries were therefore labelled broken:true on the strength of an ordinary French or Italian word in their own locale. Those labels are retracted here (see each entry notes[], prefixed "homograph-marker-retracted-2026-08-10"); no other label was touched, and no entry was deleted. Eighteen entries were added covering the corrected families and, symmetrically, the German words that share each corrected rule and must keep firing.
revisions.caveat: Because the retracted labels were false negatives for the corrected detector and true positives for the old one, recall and precision measured against this file are NOT comparable across the revision. Both detectors were re-scored against the corrected labels; the numbers are in the PR body.
